newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: HOWARD CONTENT WITH SLOW PROGRESS ON GREENHOUSE ISSUE
Prime Minister John Howard says he doesn't expect to radically change the attitude of the United States administration towards binding uniform greenhouse gas emission targets.
Mr Howard believes he's already made progress and is pleased at the response he's received from Republicans and Democrats during talks in Washington.
He's been meeting with the US House of Representatives Speaker, the Senate majority leader and over lunch with a handful of Congressional and Administration members.
Mr Howard is due to meet US President Clinton in a few hours.
While Mr Howard believes there has been movement in the Administration's position, he says it would be unrealistic to shift the attitude in one go.
Mr Howard has also received a repeated re-assurance the US will do all it can not to hurt Australia when using agricultural export subsidies.
AUSTRALIANS WORKING HARDER
Bureau of Statistics figures released today show at least one third of Australians are working harder than they were a year ago.
The latest Employment Experience statistics for the 12 months to November show 93 per cent of Australians experienced some change in their job during the year.
More than a third of those said the change was taking on more responsibilities at work, while others had taken on new or extra duties.

Middle management may have been subject to wholesale redundancies in the past decade, but the Bureau of Statistics figures show managers and administrators have at least one advantage - they were promoted more than any other class of worker during the year.
MINCHIN DEFENDS NATIVE TITLE BILL
Federal Parliamentary Secretary Nick Minchin says it's wrong to claim the Government is intent on completing the final theft of land from Aborigines.
He says there is a lot for Aborigines in draft legislation, released today, which responds to the High Court's Wik ruling on native title.
Aboriginal leaders say indigenous people are the only stakeholders to have gained nothing.
They say the legislation proposes to severely wind back the existing right to negotiate, effectively rendering the principle of native title meaningless.
But Nick Minchin says this is fiction, because the government is not providing for the blanket extinguishment of native title on pastoral leases.
He says native title can continue to be claimed on up to 78 percent of the Australian mainland, subject to the common law.
BHP PROFITS PLUNGE PROMPTS SELL-OFF WARNING
BHP has repeated warnings that it will sell businesses that don't perform satisfactorily, as part of a strategic review of operations.
Huge write-downs have seen this year's annual profit plunge more than 60 per cent, to $410 million.
A sweeping review of company assets has led to write-downs in its mineral, copper and petroleum divisions, plus a $220 million charge for plant closures and redundancy pay-outs in steel.
The total abnormal loss is more than $970 million.
Leaving aside the skewing effect of abnormals, profits were still up to six per cent down in each of minerals, copper and steel, partly due to lower metal prices.
Profits for steel products such as bars and beams, at sites including Newcastle which is to close, came in at just $48 million, compared to $260 million for sheet-steel.
BHP Managing Director John Prescott says the results reflect a company in transition, and underlying results improved on last year.
UNION SAYS PUBLIC SERVICE BILL IS TOO SIMPLISTIC
Government reforms for the public service along private business lines have been attacked by the Public Sector Union as too simplistic.
Industrial Relations Minister Peter Reith says his new Public Service Bill will introduce modern employment practices and contemporary workplace standards.
The government says the public service unions were consulted in drawing up the bill, which has been referred to a parliamentary committee.
But CPSU Secretary Wendy Caird says the union believes there's not sufficient accountability in the model presented by Mr Reith.

She says if billions of tax payer dollars are being spent on programs, there must also be the certainty there is honesty, scrutiny and open processes which go far beyond what applies in the private sector.
HOPES FOR SOLUTION TO MISSING BOY MYSTERY
Victoria's Chief Commissioner Neil Comrie is confident detectives investigating the disappearance of Jaidyn Leskie will bring about a conclusion shortly.
Mr Comrie has praised police for their patience and professionalism in investigating the abduction case, now into its 13th day.
Meanwhile, the number of police, SES volunteers and Freemasons searching the Moe tip tomorrow will grow to around 100 and a police helicopter may also be used to scan local waterways.
Baby clothes have been pulled from the rubbish today but have already been ruled out of the investigation.
Search Co Ordinator Senior Constable Oscar Aertssen says offers of help from local residents has been overwhelming.
